steps.explanationAfterStep: The forward Diels–Alder exactly reversed: two σ bonds and a π bond become three π bonds, round the same six-membered cyclic transition state. Breaking two σ bonds costs energy, so the reaction needs heat; it wins at high temperature because one molecule becomes two (entropy). Cyclopentadiene boils at 41 °C, far below the dimer, so it distils out of the hot flask and cannot recombine.

title: Cracking dicyclopentadiene
subtitle: A retro-Diels–Alder reaction gives back two cyclopentadienes
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34
Fleming, Pericyclic Reactions, 2nd edition (Oxford Chemistry Primers, Oxford University Press)

dimer.caption: dicyclopentadiene (the endo dimer)
hintTiers: This is a Diels–Alder reaction run backwards. Find the cyclohexene ring that the forward reaction made: which two σ bonds of that ring were the new ones?

The two σ bonds that break join the bridged ring to the cyclopentene ring. The C=C in the bridged ring moves outwards, and a new C=C appears where the two σ bonds were. Three arrows round the six-membered ring.

Arrow 1: from the C=C of the bridged ring to the bond between one of its carbons and the bridgehead next to it. Arrow 2: from the σ bond between the other bridgehead and the cyclopentene ring to the bond between that bridgehead and its alkene neighbour. Arrow 3: from the remaining breaking σ bond to the bond between the two cyclopentene ring carbons that were joined to the bridged ring.
dimer.learnerPrompt: On heating, the dimer falls apart into two cyclopentadiene molecules in one step. Draw every arrow of that step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The CH₂ bridge stays: it is part of the cyclopentadiene that comes off. The bonds that break are the two that join the two five-membered rings.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: one of the bonds that the forward Diels–Alder made breaks and becomes a C=C. In the same step the other one breaks too, and the C=C of the bridged ring shifts. Two more arrows.

mechanismSummary: Cyclopentadiene is so reactive a diene that it dimerises at room temperature: one molecule is the diene, the other's C=C the dienophile, and the endo adduct forms. So it is sold as the dimer and “cracked” before use: heating to about 170 °C runs the retro-Diels–Alder reaction, and the monomer is distilled off and used at once or kept cold. Retro-Diels–Alder reactions are favoured by heat because ΔS is positive (one molecule gives two) and by removing a volatile or very stable product (N₂, CO₂, an aromatic ring) in other examples. The endo geometry of the dimer is explained, not drawn. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges.
